title: Magdala to the Sainte-Baume: the Seven Devils, the Empty Tomb, and the Thirty Years in the Grotto
years: c. AD 10 – AD 72 (the relic disputes run to AD 1279)
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Magdala on the Galilee: the Seven Devils Cast Out

stops.name: Magdala: the castle of Magdalo, her lineage
stops.campa: Mary is born of a lineage the Golden Legend calls royal: her father Cyrus, her mother Eucharis, landholders of Galilee and Judea. The inheritance divides three ways among the children: Lazarus takes the portion in Jerusalem, Martha the estate at Bethany, and Mary the fishing town on the western shore of the lake, the castle of Magdalo, whence she is called Magdalene. She grows up rich, fair, and, the tradition does not soften it, given over to the pleasures her wealth affords her, in the town that will one day carry only her own name.
suggested_refs: Magdala (Migdal) archaeological site and synagogue on the Sea of Galilee shore
Georges de La Tour, The Penitent Magdalen

stops.name: Magdala, the seven devils cast out
stops.campa: Luke names her plainly among the women who follow the Teacher: Mary called Magdalene, out of whom went seven devils. The Gospel gives no more than the fact and lets the number stand for whatever completeness of ruin a soul can hold: seven, the number of the whole. Jesus speaks, and the multitude of spirits goes out of her at once, not one by one. She does not return to the pleasures of Magdala. She turns instead and follows the man who emptied her, and gives what she owns to the work of his kingdom.
suggested_refs: the seven-branched motif in later Magdalene iconography
the ointment jar as her identifying emblem in Christian art

stops.name: Cana of Galilee, witness to the first sign
stops.campa: Among the guests at the wedding in Cana, where the wine fails and the stone jars of water are filled to the brim at Mary the mother's word, the newly healed woman of Magdala stands with the small company that has begun to gather around the Teacher. She watches the servants draw out wine where there had been only well-water, watches the astonishment of the governor of the feast. It is the first sign, and she is present at it, one of the company who will follow this abundance all the way to the far end of loss and back again.
suggested_refs: Wedding Church at Cana (Kafr Kanna)
Giotto, Marriage at Cana (Scrovegni Chapel)
sources: jesus.journey.json (shared pin, the first sign at Cana)

stops.name: Capernaum: the sinful woman's tears, a tradition folded into her
stops.campa: At the house of a Pharisee, the Gospel does not name the town; the West's long tradition sets the scene here in Capernaum, where a woman known through the city as a sinner comes in uninvited, weeping, and stands behind him at the table. She washes his feet with her tears, dries them with her unbound hair, and anoints them from an alabaster box, while the Pharisee looks on in scorn. He tells her that her sins are forgiven, for she loved much. Centuries of the Latin church will fold this woman into Magdalene herself, though the Gospel never gives her a name.
suggested_refs: the alabaster ointment jar of Magdalene iconography
Peter Paul Rubens, Christ in the House of Simon the Pharisee
sources: Gregory the Great, Homily 33 (the medieval conflation of the sinner, Mary of Bethany, and Mary Magdalene)

stops.name: The Sea of Galilee: Joanna, Susanna, and the provisioning of the Twelve
stops.campa: Luke sets her name beside two others seldom heard again, Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza, and Susanna, and says only that these, and many more, minister to him of their own substance. It is the plainest sentence in the Gospel and the largest one: a company of women, some of means, fund the Teacher's traveling household out of their own purses, cook, carry, and keep the Twelve fed on the road between towns. Mary of Magdala, once emptied of seven devils, becomes one of the hands that keeps the kingdom's business running while the men are sent out to preach it.
suggested_refs: the Galilee boat (first-century fishing boat) at Kibbutz Ginosar

stops.name: Mount of Beatitudes, hearing the Sermon
stops.campa: On the green hill above the lake she sits among the crowd that has followed him up from the shore and hears the new law given: blessed are the poor, the mourning, the meek, the merciful, the persecuted. She who was cast out of herself by seven devils and given back whole hears the promise made first to those the world discards. Whatever she carries away from the mountain that day, she will carry it all the way to a grotto in another country, thirty years from now, where meekness and mourning become the whole of her daily bread.
suggested_refs: Church of the Beatitudes on the Mount of Beatitudes
sources: jesus.journey.json (shared pin, the Sermon on the Mount)

stops.name: Nain, witnessing the raising of the widow's son
stops.campa: At the gate of Nain a dead man is carried out on a bier, the only son of a widow, and Jesus stops the funeral with a single word: Young man, arise. Among the women who witness it, tradition places Mary of Magdala, watching a mother's mourning turned in an instant into a mother's son restored. She has already been given back her own life once, emptied of what possessed her; now she watches him give a whole widowed house its life back too, and understands a little more of what following this man will mean, and what it will someday cost her.
suggested_refs: the village of Nein (Nain) on the slope of the Hill of Moreh
sources: jesus.journey.json (shared pin, the raising at Nain)

segments.name: Bethany and the Road Up: the Brother Raised, the Body Anointed

stops.name: Bethany: the raising of Lazarus, her brother
stops.campa: Lazarus lies four days in the tomb, and his sister goes out to meet the Teacher on the road before he even reaches the house: Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died. It is the same sentence Martha has already spoken, word for word, and the Western church will read both sisters as one woman under two names: Mary of Bethany folded into Mary of Magdala. Whichever telling is followed, she stands at the tomb mouth when the stone is rolled back and hears the four-days-dead man called out of the dark by his own name.
stops.quote: Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.
suggested_refs: the Tomb of Lazarus at Bethany (Al-Eizariya)
Giotto, Raising of Lazarus (Scrovegni Chapel)
sources: jesus.journey.json (shared pin, the raising of Lazarus)
Gregory the Great, Homily 33 (the conflation of Mary of Bethany and Mary Magdalene)

stops.name: Jericho: on the road up, Bartimaeus and Zacchaeus
stops.campa: On the road up out of Jericho, in the press that surrounds blind Bartimaeus crying for mercy and gathers beneath the sycamore where the tax-man Zacchaeus has climbed to see him, Mary of Magdala walks among the company going up to Jerusalem for the last time. She has followed this road for four years now, Galilee to Judea and back, provisioning, watching, learning what the kingdom costs its own. Ahead lies the city, the Passover, and the single week the Gospels will remember longer than almost any other week in the whole history of the world.
suggested_refs: the sycamore of Zacchaeus, Jericho

stops.name: Bethany, the anointing at Simon's house
stops.campa: Six days before the Passover, at supper in the house of Simon, Mary takes a pound of costly spikenard and anoints the Teacher's feet, wiping them with her unbound hair until the whole house is filled with the fragrance. Judas objects that it might have fed the poor; Jesus answers that she has kept this against the day of his burying, and that wherever the Gospel is preached this deed will be told for a memorial of her. Whether this Mary is the sister of Lazarus or the woman once healed at Magdala, the tradition does not fully untangle the two, and does not need to.
suggested_refs: Bethany (Al-Eizariya), house of Simon the Leper
the alabaster jar of nard, her attribute in art
sources: jesus.journey.json (shared pin, the anointing at Bethany)

segments.name: The Passion Watch and the Dawn

stops.name: Golgotha, standing at the cross
stops.campa: Many of the disciples have fled; the women do not. Mark names her first among those who stand and watch from a distance while the cross is lifted: Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joses, and Salome. She has followed him from Galilee, ministering to him with her own hands, and she does not leave now that ministry can no longer help him: only watch, through the three hours of darkness, through the cry of dereliction, through the last breath and the tearing of the Temple veil, to an end that is not, though no one there yet knows it, the end.
suggested_refs: the Rock of Calvary in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
medieval Crucifixion panels showing the Magdalene at the foot of the cross

stops.name: The Tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, the burial watched
stops.campa: Joseph of Arimathea takes the body down at evening, and Mary Magdalene and the other Mary sit over against the sepulchre and watch where he is laid: the Gospel's own word, beholding, as if seeing itself were now the only service left to give. She marks the rock, the garden, the great stone rolled to the door, because she means to come back the moment the Sabbath allows it, with spices, to do for the body what Friday's haste did not allow. She is the last to leave the tomb that night, and, though she cannot know it yet, will be the first to return to it.
suggested_refs: the Edicule of the Holy Sepulchre over the Tomb of Christ

stops.name: The Sabbath, preparing the spices
stops.campa: The Sabbath falls over Jerusalem like a held breath, and the law forbids all labor, even the labor of grief. Mary and the other women rest, as the commandment requires, and prepare what they can before sundown: the spices and ointments bought or set aside, kept ready for the one thing the law cannot forbid once the sun goes down a second time. She anointed his feet with nard while he lived; now she means to anoint the whole body in death, and the waiting through this one silent day is its own kind of vigil, spent in the house at Bethany among the mourning women.
suggested_refs: the spice-merchants of the Jerusalem markets named in the Passion narratives

stops.name: The Garden Tomb: the empty tomb, Easter morning
stops.campa: Very early, while it is yet dark, she comes to the tomb with spices and finds the stone already rolled away. She runs first, not to look inside, but to Peter and to the beloved disciple, with the only sentence she can form: they have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and she does not know where they have laid him. The men run back with her and find it just as she said, and go home again believing only that the body is gone. Mary stays behind, weeping at the mouth of an empty grave. She is the one who does not leave the garden.
stops.quote: They have taken away my Lord, and I know not where they have laid him.
suggested_refs: the Empty Tomb (Edicule) in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
the Anastasis icon (Harrowing of Hell)

stops.name: The Garden: Noli me tangere, apostle to the apostles
stops.campa: Weeping still, she turns and sees a man she takes for the gardener. Woman, why weepest thou? Whom seekest thou? She answers, still not knowing him. Then he speaks one word, her own name, Mary, and everything turns over at once. Rabboni, she cries, and reaches for him; he tells her not to hold him, for he is not yet ascended, but to go and tell his brethren. She runs to the eleven with the sentence the Church will never let go of: I have seen the Lord. The apostle to the apostles delivers the first Easter word ever spoken, to the men who are meant to be preaching it to her.
stops.quote: Rabboni... I have seen the Lord.
suggested_refs: the Noli me tangere garden tradition
Titian, Noli me Tangere
Fra Angelico, Noli Me Tangere (San Marco)
sources: jesus.journey.json (shared pin, the risen Lord to Mary Magdalene)

segments.name: The Years After: Pentecost to the Rudderless Boat

stops.name: Jerusalem, the Upper Room: Pentecost
stops.campa: In the upper room on Mount Zion, the same house where the bread was broken seven weeks before, Mary Magdalene continues with the eleven, with Jesus's mother, and with the other women in prayer, of one accord, waiting on the promise. When the day of Pentecost is fully come, the sound comes like a mighty rushing wind, and tongues of fire sit upon each of them, and they speak in tongues not their own. The apostle to the apostles receives the same fire as the apostles she once outran to the tomb: the Spirit, descending, does not ask who ran there first.
suggested_refs: the Cenacle, Mount Zion
the icon of Pentecost, with the Mother of God enthroned among the apostles

stops.name: Jerusalem: the persecution after Stephen, the scattering
stops.campa: Stephen is stoned outside the walls, and a great persecution rises against the young church at Jerusalem; Saul of Tarsus goes from house to house dragging out men and women. The company that gathered at Pentecost scatters into Judea, Samaria, and farther. Tradition holds that Mary Magdalene, with Lazarus and Martha her own household, and Maximin and others of the seventy-two disciples, are among those the authorities single out: too visible, too closely tied to the empty tomb and the risen Teacher, to be let go quietly. They are seized, and a harder road than any in Galilee opens ahead of them.
suggested_refs: the traditional site of Stephen's martyrdom outside the Damascus Gate

stops.name: Jaffa, cast to sea without oar, sail, or rudder
stops.campa: At the coast the persecutors put them into a ship without sail, oar, or rudder, meaning to drown a whole household of the new faith at once: Mary Magdalene, Lazarus, Martha, Maximin, Martha's chamberer Marcella, the blind man Cedonius whom Christ had healed from birth, and Sarah, an Egyptian handmaid attached to the company. They are pushed out onto open water with no means of steering and no means of returning. The sea that once fell still at a word from the Teacher is now asked, without a word from anyone aboard, to carry his friends home to it.
suggested_refs: the port of Jaffa (Joppa), traditional point of departure
sources: the Provençal Vita Beatae Mariae Magdalenae

segments.name: The Camargue Landing and the Marseille Cycle

stops.name: Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer, the miraculous landing
stops.campa: Without oar or sail or any hand to steer it, the boat crosses the whole width of the sea and runs aground on a low shingle shore at the mouth of the Rhône, where the Camargue's salt flats meet the tide. The company comes ashore into a country whose language none of them speak, in the place the centuries will call Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer for the women who landed there. Sarah, the Egyptian servant, will be kept by the region's memory as patroness of all who wander without a country of their own. Her feast still gathers pilgrims to this same beach every May.
suggested_refs: the fortified church of Notre-Dame-de-la-Mer, Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer
the crypt and shrine of Sainte Sara, patroness of the Roma pilgrimage

stops.name: Marseille: preaching to the pagans, the prince and princess's vow
stops.campa: In the old Greek port of Marseille, Mary Magdalene preaches to a people who sacrifice to idols, denouncing their worship with the same directness she once heard turned on her own sins. The prince who governs the city and his wife, childless and desperate, come to her by night; she tells them plainly that their gods can give them nothing, and that only the God whose empty tomb she witnessed can open a barren womb. The princess sees her three times in visions before the couple, still unconverted, strikes the bargain that will carry them across the sea to test the claim against Peter himself in Rome.
suggested_refs: the Vieux-Port of Marseille, ancient Massalia
Notre-Dame-de-la-Garde overlooking the harbor

stops.name: The rock off Marseille: the storm, the princess's death
stops.campa: The prince and his pregnant wife take ship for Rome to put the Magdalene's word to Peter, and a violent storm catches them at sea. The princess goes into labor in the tempest, bears a son, and dies of the ordeal before the ship can make any harbor. The sailors, unwilling to keep two corpses and a living infant aboard, set the dead mother and the child ashore together on a bare rock and sail on without them, leaving the prince to weep over a wife he cannot bury and a son he cannot feed, on a stone in the middle of the open sea.
suggested_refs: the legendary rock of the shipwreck, traditionally placed off the Marseille coast

stops.name: Rome and Jerusalem, the prince's two years with Peter
stops.campa: The prince goes on to Rome alone and finds Peter, who confirms every word Mary Magdalene preached and takes him on to Jerusalem to walk the ground of the Passion and the empty tomb for two full years. All the while, on the rock where he left them, the dead woman's body lies uncorrupted and her infant son lives and thrives, nursed, the tradition insists, by the invisible care of the very saint whose word set this whole voyage in motion. The prince returns believing everything, not yet knowing how literally the promise of provision has been kept for him.
suggested_refs: Old St Peter's basilica, Rome, where the prince's faith is confirmed

stops.name: The rock off Marseille: the return, the princess revived
stops.campa: Two years to the day, the ship passes the rock again and the prince finds his son alive and playing at the water's edge, kept whole by a power he cannot see. Falling to his knees he prays to the Magdalene by name to finish what she began: she who has fed and kept his son two years in this rock, let her restore also the boy's mother. The dead woman draws breath, opens her eyes, and rises as from ordinary sleep, telling of a pilgrimage of her own soul that ran, mile for mile, beside her husband's the whole two years, unseen by him.
suggested_refs: the Prince and Princess of Marseille cycle in medieval Magdalene iconography

stops.name: Marseille, the baptism of the prince and princess
stops.campa: The family returns rejoicing to Marseille and finds Lazarus, Mary Magdalene, and the rest of the company still at their preaching. The prince and princess destroy the idols of the city with their own hands and receive baptism from Maximin, becoming the first fruits of a Provence that will, in the centuries to come, count itself Christian from this very hour. Mary Magdalene, who arrived on a rudderless boat with nothing, now stands godmother to a whole converted household and, through them, to a coastline. Her preaching in the city complete, she turns her face toward the wilder country inland.
suggested_refs: the Vieux-Port of Marseille and its early Christian foundation legends

segments.name: Tarascon, the Ground of Saint-Gilles, and the Grotto

stops.name: Tarascon, Sainte-Marthe and the Tarasque
stops.campa: Martha, restless in Marseille's shadow, goes up the Rhône to Tarascon, where a beast called the Tarasque, part lion, part dragon, part ox, has been laying waste to the countryside from its den by the river. She goes out to it alone, holy water and a cross in hand, and it lies down before her like a lamb; she binds it with her own girdle and leads it into the town, where the terrified people kill it on the spot and beg her to stay and preach. Mary blesses her sister's going before Martha ever sees the beast, and the two do not meet again in the flesh.
suggested_refs: the collegiate church of Sainte-Marthe at Tarascon, over the tomb of the hostess of Christ
the Tarasque effigy carried in the Tarascon fêtes
sources: Legenda Aurea, ch. 105 (the Life of Saint Martha)
pica_bourlemont.journey.json (shared pin, Tarascon, Sainte-Marthe and the rule of the rose)

stops.name: The Camargue near Saint-Gilles, the ground before the hermitage
stops.campa: Following the Rhône down toward its mouth, Mary Magdalene crosses a stretch of wild delta country, thicket, thorn, and a clear spring, a country that as yet has no name and no hermit in it. Six hundred years will pass before a Greek exile called Giles finds this same ground, builds his cave beside this same water, and gives the place the name it will keep forever. She does not know she is walking through another saint's future address; the corpus folds its own time here, honestly, the way it must: Giles arrives on her ground long after she has already left it behind.
suggested_refs: the crypt and cave of the Abbey of Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, later built on this ground
sources: giles.journey.json (shared pin, the forest of the Vallée Flavienne)

stops.name: La Sainte-Baume: the grotto, the retreat begins
stops.campa: Above the wooded gorge east of Marseille, in the massif the country will call the Sainte-Baume, the holy cave, Mary Magdalene finds a fissure in the white rock, high above any road, and goes into it to stay. No spring reaches it, no tree grows near it, no herb softens the stone. She leaves the world of preaching and conversion behind entirely, the way she once left Magdala, and gives herself instead to thirty years of a penance so total that the tradition will not even grant her the ordinary mercy of running water.
suggested_refs: the Grotte de la Sainte-Baume, Plan-d'Aups-Sainte-Baume
the Dominican sanctuary built into the cliff face

stops.name: La Sainte-Baume, lifted by angels at the seven hours
stops.campa: Every day at the seven canonical hours, matins, lauds, the day offices, vespers, compline, angels lift her bodily into the air of the cave, and she hears with her own ears the song of the heavenly companies that no living mortal is otherwise permitted to hear from the ground. This is her whole nourishment: no bread, no water, only what the choirs give her at each hour, carried up and set down again like a tide that never wets her feet. A hermit priest, coming near enough once to see it, tells no one for years, not fully trusting his own eyes.
suggested_refs: the depiction of the Magdalene lifted by angels in Provençal Gothic sculpture and stained glass

stops.name: La Sainte-Baume, the vision granted to Maximin
stops.campa: Word finally reaches Maximin, now bishop, of the hermit priest's vision, and Maximin comes himself to see: in the cave he watches her lifted the height of two or three cubits from the floor, hands raised among a company of angels, her face lit as though the sun itself were shining through the rock behind her. He understands, watching, that thirty years have very nearly run their course, and that he is not seeing a woman merely fed by heaven so much as a woman being finished by it, made ready at last for whatever door the last hour opens for her.
suggested_refs: the vision of Maximin in the Sainte-Baume cycle of Provençal art

segments.name: The Last Communion and the Two Tombs

stops.name: Saint-Maximin (Villalata): the last communion, her death
stops.campa: Told beforehand by the Lord of her approaching end, Mary Magdalene leaves the cave for the last time and comes down to Maximin's oratory at Villalata, the town that will one day take his name. There, angels bear her, one final time, into the church itself, and set her before the altar where Maximin waits with the sacrament. He gives her communion with his own hands; she makes her prayer with her hands joined, and rests in peace. A great brightness fills the whole oratory at her passing, and a sweet odor lingers in the place for seven days afterward, as if thirty years of silence had one last thing left to say.
suggested_refs: the crypt believed to hold the skull relic of Mary Magdalene, Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume

stops.name: Vézelay: the rival tomb, held unreconciled
stops.campa: A millennium removed from Villalata, a Burgundian hilltop abbey opens a wholly different chapter of the same devotion: the monks of Vézelay declare that they hold Mary Magdalene's true relics, carried north, some say from Aix, some say by a monk fleeing Saracen raids on the Provençal coast, and enshrine them beneath a great new Romanesque nave. Pilgrims by the tens of thousands come to Burgundy believing they kneel before the same bones that Provence also claims to keep whole in its own crypt. Both traditions stand, and neither is debunked here; this corpus does not choose between them.
suggested_refs: the Basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine, Vézelay, and its Romanesque tympanum
sources: Victor Saxer, Le culte de Marie Madeleine en Occident

stops.name: Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, the 1279 translation of the relics
stops.campa: Two centuries after Vézelay's claim, Charles II of Anjou, count of Provence, comes in person to the crypt at Saint-Maximin and has the tomb opened before witnesses: the skull is found separate from the rest, still bearing, they report, a fragment of desiccated flesh on the brow, where the risen Christ is said to have once told her not to touch him: the noli me tangere kept, quite literally, in the bone. Charles commissions a new Gothic basilica over the site and gives the relic its own reliquary bust. Provence's claim, like Burgundy's, is neither proven nor surrendered; the two tombs simply go on, each keeping its own vigil.
suggested_refs: the reliquary bust and crypt at the Basilica of Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume
the 1279 translation ceremony of Charles II of Anjou
sources: Victor Saxer, Le culte de Marie Madeleine en Occident
